name: Hay's Maroon
lede: Hay's Maroon is a dark, greyed reddish brown from Robert Ridgway's 1912 color dictionary, one of six colors he names for a person called only Hay.

sections.title: One of six colors named Hay's
sections.body:
Ridgway's 1912 “Color Standards and Color Nomenclature” lists Hay's Maroon at hex #654543 among the names he credits to a person [1]. It shares its possessive with five other colors in the same book, among them [[hay-s-brown|Hay's Brown]], [[hay-s-green|Hay's Green]] and [[hay-s-russet|Hay's Russet]], but Ridgway never names the Hay he means, so the connection is undocumented in our sources [1]. The 1955 Inter-Society Color Council catalog repeats the name in the block it calls grayish reddish brown [1].

Its nearest neighbor in our color graph is [[liver|Liver]], only 3.2 units away and redder [1]. [[dark-perilla-purple|Dark Perilla Purple]] sits almost as close [1]. Against the basic color words it reads closest to [[umber|Umber]], 8.4 units off [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive matches this color in 1.42% of 23,781 paintings, 338 of them, as photographed; the within-painting lens finds it in 214 [2]. That makes it more common than 72% of the named colors in our set [2]. It peaks in the 1900s, present in 2.6% of the 1,674 paintings from that century, 2.4 times the rate its museums would predict [2]. Inside a painting it most often sits hidden, in 61% of its 214 appearances [2]. John Singer Sargent holds it in 6 of his 287 works here, though at that rate no painter stands out sharply against the museum baseline [2]. Our earliest match dates to 1270, by the Master of the Franciscan Crucifixes, 642 years before Ridgway's 1912 book recorded the name, a floor rather than a first, since a color match in an aged photograph is not proof of a pigment [2].
